What started as a slow, cautious experiment has accelerated. By late 2025, the company began operating internationally and performing simultaneous surgeries. 96 Most notably, the learning curve has collapsed. While early patients required significant training, recent recipients in Canada achieved control of the system within minutes of activation. 97 We are now witnessing a move beyond the screen. The next phase of trials aims to bridge the digital back to the physical, using these same neural signals to control robotic arms. The implications are profound: a future where the bandwidth of our thoughts is no longer limited by the speed of our fingers, but only by the speed of our imagination. Today, we largely use AI on screens. It is moving from wearable, frequently available AI toward ambient, always available AI. And perhaps one day, the screen goes away altogether, and we interact with AI simply through thought. The Dunning–Kruger Effect One of the more humbling discoveries in cognitive science is the Dunning–Kruger effect—a well-documented psychological bias in which individuals with only rudimentary knowledge or competence in a domain tend to overestimate their knowledge or competence, while experts often underestimate theirs. 98 I think of the Dunning–Kruger effect as the biological analogy of AI hallucinations. The paradox here is that, in order to know how much you don’t know, you must already know enough to grasp the complexity of the topic. Until now, overcoming this effect for any given domain required years of study, exposure to domain experts, and iterative feedback. But that’s beginning to change. With the advent of conversational AI systems, we now have a way to dramatically accelerate the acquisition of domain knowledge—not by bypassing effort, but by augmenting it with immediate, interactive guidance. Instead of lingering for years in overconfidence or false certainty, a curious mind can now partner with a system that challenges assumptions, surfaces deeper principles, and nudges the learner toward a more calibrated understanding. My Own Dunning–Kruger Moment In the early 2000s, I became friends with Kimbal Musk when helping him raise $5 million for a start-up company, where I sat on his board for a year. Kimbal was gracious enough to give me a copy of the Tesla Series B funding materials. I did not end up participating in that round (big mistake!), but Kimbal still invited me to dinner with him and his brother, Elon, and three other people in Los Angeles at the launch of the Tesla Roadster. Elon was a wildly successful entrepreneur by then, but he had not yet achieved the recognition that he has today as perhaps the greatest visionary entrepreneur alive. Over dinner, my Dunning–Kruger moment was in full swing as I challenged Elon about the battery deterioration problem. My knowledge was directionally accurate, but I was not up to speed on the progress that was being made. Elon simply told me that they would be fine and dismissed the debate. Damn, I wish I’d had Claude back then to help me prepare for that dinner more thoughtfully. In this sense, AI is not just a tool—it is an extension of our epistemic reach. A kind of cognitive prosthetic that can help us overcome some of the inherent biases of the human mind. From this perspective, AI is not separate from us but an extension of us. It has the potential to take us far beyond anywhere we could go with our energy constraints. Or to leave us behind. And in some ways, it depends on how we plug into it. “My AI Told Me …” While the rise of AI agents embedded in every layer of software—from CRM systems to scheduling apps to autonomous infrastructure—is already well underway, I believe we’re missing something even bigger. As useful as these agents will be, they are not what people will build lasting emotional bonds with. What’s coming next—perhaps faster than we expect—is the emergence of personal AI companions that people return to again and again. These AIs will not be buried in apps or reduced to task managers. They will become trusted thought partners. Mirrors. Coaches. Therapists. Collaborators. Friends. We’ll still rely on specialized AI agents to book our travel, sort our email, or coordinate team workflows. But when it comes to the most meaningful interactions—identity, growth, perspective, and memory—people will increasingly turn to their personal AI. It will know their history, hold their context, understand their preferences, and evolve alongside them in tone, trust, and even affection. This is not sci-fi. It’s already beginning. When people say, “I asked my AI …” or “My AI told me …,” they’re not just referring to a query result. They’re describing a relationship. And that relationship has stickiness unlike anything we’ve seen in the history of software. Once someone has a deep, consistent dialogue with an AI that knows them really well, they are going to be highly reluctant to switch to another. The switching cost isn’t technical—it’s emotional. It’s like switching therapists or abandoning a journal that’s been with you for years. And the companies that recognize this now—those that prioritize continuity, emotional resonance, and deep user context—will be the ones that define the next era of human–computer interaction. You may recall that when OpenAI released ChatGPT 5, it was more capable but less emotionally engaging, and the response was urgent calls to “bring back my AI.” This has profound implications for the market. In the early 2000s, Google became the defining winner of the search engine era. It wasn’t the only search engine—it was just the one people trusted most, used first, and returned to by default. It became a verb. And once that loyalty was locked in, it was nearly impossible to dislodge. Companion AI will follow the same pattern—but even more deeply.
